analysis.one_liner: Gives college athletes the right to unionize and collectively bargain over pay and working conditions.
analysis.headline: A bill giving college athletes union bargaining rights was referred to committee and died there, never receiving a vote in the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal labor law so that college athletes who are paid, or whose scholarships require them to play, count as employees. They could then form unions and bargain collectively with their schools, with schools in an athletic conference negotiating as one unit. It would also apply federal labor law to public universities, which are normally exempt, and forbid any agreement that makes athletes give up these rights. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes who receive scholarships or other direct compensation tied to playing a sport. They would gain the right to organize unions and negotiate over compensation, hours, health and safety protections, and other conditions—rights professional athletes already have. Because conferences could bargain as one unit, athletes would not be forced to negotiate school by school. The bill also ensures coverage at public universities, where state-law exemptions currently leave many athletes outside federal labor protections.

how_it_helps.text: Defines college athletes who receive direct compensation tied to playing a sport as employees, letting them unionize and bargain collectively over pay and working conditions.
Extends National Labor Relations Board jurisdiction to public universities for college athletes, closing a gap that otherwise leaves athletes at state schools without federal labor-law protection.
Lets athletes at schools in the same athletic conference bargain as one unit, so schools cannot play them against each other.
Prohibits scholarship agreements that force athletes to waive their right to collectively bargain, and bars settlements that allow noncompliance.

analysis.who_pays: The NCAA, athletic conferences, and member universities, which would lose unilateral control over the terms of athletes' labor and face collective bargaining over compensation and working conditions. Taxpayers at public universities could indirectly share in those added costs.

drawbacks.text: Requiring public universities to bargain collectively under federal labor law would raise labor costs for athletic departments, and schools might respond by cutting non-revenue sports or shifting costs elsewhere.

Treating athletes as employees of a conference-wide bargaining unit raises hard design questions—such as how to reconcile bargaining with different state laws and with students' academic status—that the bill never had a chance to be refined or debated, since it died in committee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit—giving college athletes real bargaining power over pay, health, and safety—would come at a real cost to the college sports industry, which would share more of its revenue with the athletes who generate it. That shift in bargaining power is the point of the bill, not a flaw. Genuine design questions remain about how to bargain for a workforce that is also a student body, but Congress never considered them: the bill died in committee before any hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 15, 2021 by Rep. Jamaal Bowman and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The NCAA, athletic conferences, and universities keep full control over college athletes' compensation and working conditions, with no collective bargaining obligation. Athletes gain nothing.

for.name: Rep. Jamaal Bowman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give college athletes collective bargaining rights.

for.name: Reps. Andy Levin and Lori Trahan
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral—no hearing, no markup, no vote—so the bill never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three sponsors were all House Democrats; no Republican cosponsor ever joined, and the Democratic-controlled committee never moved it.

industries.industry: NCAA, athletic conferences, and college sports programs
industries.note: Athletes would gain the right to bargain collectively over pay and conditions, ending a system the bill's findings describe as caps on compensation justified by 'amateurism.' Schools and conferences would no longer be able to unilaterally set the terms of athletes' labor.

Public institutions would become employers under the National Labor Relations Act for college athletes, facing bargaining obligations they do not currently bear. Athletes at state schools, currently outside federal labor law, would gain coverage.
